passage: Note by Pallavi, catering supervisor, on Aditi, a trainee running a wedding lunch for 200 guests. Aditi spent extra time at the start on three things: checking that the allergy labels matched the dishes, counting the cash till, and confirming the gas connection was secure. Aditi told me these things "can't be undone". The napkin folds were done quickly, and a few came out uneven. The table numbers were handwritten, not printed. Nobody noticed. Aditi had time left to stand at the door and greet guests. I want the whole trainee group to learn this ordering of effort. - Pallavi

qa.q: Which three things did Aditi check carefully at the start?
qa.a: Aditi checked that the allergy labels matched the dishes, counted the cash till and confirmed the gas connection was secure.

qa.q: Why did Aditi not worry about the uneven napkin folds?
qa.a: Aditi felt calm about them, since napkins are easy to overlook or fix, unlike safety and money, which can't be undone.

qa.q: What rule of thumb could other trainees take from Aditi?
qa.a: Spend care on safety, money and anything hard to undo, and let the rest be good enough.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Aditi's ordering of effort?
qa.a: Pallavi sees it as a good model and wants the whole trainee group to learn it.

grounding: Shows a worker who puts care into safety, money and things hard to undo and lets the rest be good enough.

passage: Thursday. Big lesson today from Pankaj. We were preparing the monthly payroll run and a slide deck for Friday. I was about to spend the afternoon on the deck's animations. Pankaj asked, "What can't we undo?" The payroll: once it is sent, the money is gone. So we checked the totals twice, compared them with last month, and had a second person read the account numbers. The deck? Fifteen minutes, plain, done. It was bare but clear, and nobody complained. I realised I had been giving everything the same effort and finishing nothing early. - Irfan

qa.q: How did Irfan feel about the lesson from Pankaj?
qa.a: Irfan seems humbled and grateful, realising that everything had been given the same effort, so nothing finished early and the most important work got no extra care.
Checking the payroll carefully and keeping the deck plain, because the effort matched the cost of failure.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj focus on the payroll?
qa.a: Because once it is sent the money is gone, so it needs the most care.

grounding: Shows a worker deciding what must be excellent, such as money and irreversible steps, and letting the rest be good enough.
